---
title: "A Room with an Ocean View"
format: html
execute:
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

Let's imagine the following scenario: in a beautiful sea-side university, there are 500 students total and 200 rooms with a beautiful view to the sea. If you are like me, you would want to have a room with a view to the sea as well. For the purpose of this simulation, let's assume everyone wants to have a room with a view to the sea. 

Because everyone wants to have a room view a view, the university has decided to allocate these special rooms through a lottery system. Students are given a random lottery number that determines the order in which they can pick their room. The earlier your number, the better your chances of getting a sea-view room.

In this simulation, I’ll model the housing lottery by randomly assigning both the order in which students pick and the rooms available. I’ll then repeat the process 200 times to estimate how likely each lottery position is to end up with a room that has a sea view. IN other words, I’ll use one function to simulate a full housing draw and a mapping function to repeat the simulation across all positions, allowing me to estimate the probability of getting a sea-view room for each possible lottery number.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

set.seed(47) # I chose 47 as the seed because of Pomona College.
library(tidyverse)

# this function runs one random housing draw 
housing_lottery <- function(total_students = 500, view_rooms = 200){
  order <- sample.int(total_students) # random lottery order
  tibble(
    order_number = 1:total_students,
    room_type = if_else(order <= view_rooms, "beautiful_view", "regular")
  )
}

#  this function will help me find how often a position gets a view room
#  (it now uses a lightweight simulation to speed things up dramatically)
position_success <- function(order_spot, trials = 200,
                             total_students = 500, view_rooms = 200){
  mean(
    replicate(trials, {
      order <- sample.int(total_students)  # random lottery order
      pick_rank <- match(order_spot, order)
      pick_rank <= view_rooms
    })
  )
}

spots <- 1:500
chance_by_spot <- map_dbl(spots, \(x) position_success(x))

results <- tibble(order_spot = spots, prob_view = chance_by_spot)

# Let's plot the results so we can better see the results of the simulation. I am using pink as the color as I like pink!
ggplot(results, aes(x = order_spot, y = prob_view)) +
  geom_line(color = "deeppink", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "deeppink", size = 0.8) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  labs(
    title = "Housing Lottery Simulation",
    subtitle = "Chance of getting a room with a beautiful view by lottery order",
    x = "Lottery order (1 = earliest pick)",
    y = "Probability of getting a room with a beautiful view"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```


From the simulation I ran, we can see that the probability of receiving a room with a sea view remains roughly in this imaginary college remains constant across all lottery positions. This occurs because both the lottery order and the room assignments are randomized, meaning each student has approximately the same chance (around 40%) of getting a sea-view room. The fluctuations in the line represent random variation between simulation runs rather than systematic differences in opportunity.
